{{Short description|Prioritizing promising moves for speed}}'''Move ordering''' refers to the practice of selecting the most promising moves first during [[Game tree|game-tree]] search (especially in [[computer chess]]).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Russell |first1=Stuart |author-link1=Stuart J. Russell |title=Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach |last2=Norvig |first2=Peter |author-link2=Peter Norvig |date=April 28, 2020 |publisher=[[Pearson Education]] |isbn=978-0134610993 |edition=4th |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |pages=152–161 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite conference |last1=Schaeffer |first1=Jonathan |author-link1=Jonathan Schaeffer |title=New Advances in Alpha-Beta Searching |last2=Plaat |first2=Aske |conference=CSC '96: Proceedings of the 1996 ACM 24th Annual Conference on Computer Science |date=February 20, 1996 |publisher=[[Association for Computing Machinery]] |isbn=0-89791-828-2 |location=Philadelphia, Pennsylvania |pages=124–130 |doi=10.1145/228329.228344 |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/228329.228344|doi-access=free }}</ref> In [[minimax]] searches with [[alpha–beta pruning]], good move ordering is important, examining stronger moves early causes cutoffs that eliminate subtrees, vastly reducing the number of nodes searched. In the ideal case of perfect move ordering the [[Time complexity|search complexity]] drops from <math>O(b^d)</math> to approximately <math>O(b^{d/2})</math>, effectively halving the effective [[branching factor]] to <math>\sqrt{b}</math> and allowing roughly twice the search [[Ply (game theory)|depth]] for a given computational effort.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Reinefeld |first1=Alexander |author-link1=Alexander Reinefeld |last2=Marsland |first2=T. Anthony |date=July 31, 1994 |title=Enhanced Iterative-Deepening Search |journal=[[IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence]] |publisher=[[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers|IEEE]] |volume=16 |issue=7 |pages=701–710 |doi=10.1109/34.297950 |bibcode=1994ITPAM..16..701R |issn=0162-8828 |eissn=1939-3539 }} Full text available at [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/3192300_Enhanced_Iterative-Deepening_Search ResearchGate] (deprecated than the original)</ref> [[Claude Shannon]] observed that although a typical chess position may have on the order of 30 legal moves, effective pruning and [[heuristic]]s reduce the useful branching factor to only a few.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Shannon |first=Claude E. |author-link=Claude Shannon |date=March 1950 |title=Programming a Computer for Playing Chess |journal=[[Philosophical Magazine]] |series=Ser. 7 |volume=41 |issue=314 |pages=256–275 |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]] |doi=10.1080/14786445008521796 |url=https://vision.unipv.it/IA1/ProgrammingaComputerforPlayingChess.pdf |language=en}}</ref>

== History ==
The idea of ordering moves came before computers. In his 1950 seminal paper "Programming a Computer for Playing Chess",{{sfn|Shannon|1950|pp=257–268}} Claude Shannon noted the enormous size of the full game tree (estimated at <math>10^{120}</math> nodes) and suggested that a simple evaluation coupled with search all variations to a fixed depth would be impractical. Shannon saw that any chess program would need to focus on selected moves and prune aggressively to be useful. The formal alpha–beta algorithm appeared in the late 1950s and 1960s as a way to prune branches without changing the minimax result. Early on, it was noted that alpha–beta's pruning power depends entirely on the order in which moves are examined. In 1963, [[Alexander Brudno]] independently described alpha–beta-like search and noted that best-case node counts occur when moves are tried in the right order; by the 1970s researchers such as [[Donald Knuth]] and [[Ronald W. Moore (computer scientist)|Ronald Moore]] had mathematically analyzed alpha–beta and shown that under perfect ordering its time is <math>O(b^{d/2})</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marsland |first=T. Anthony |date=March 1, 1986 |title=A Review of Game-Tree Pruning |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3233/ICG-1986-9102 |journal=[[ICGA Journal]] |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=3–19 |doi=10.3233/ICG-1986-9102 |issn=1389-6911 |eissn=2468-2438 |via=[[Sage Publishing|Sage Journals]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In the 1970s and 1980s the major practical heuristics for move ordering were introduced. The use of [[Iterative deepening depth-first search|iterative deepening]] was rediscovered in chess programs and found to significantly improve move ordering for deeper searches. The idea was to use the best move found at shallow depth as the first move in the next deeper search.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Knuth |first1=Donald |author-link1=Donald Knuth |last2=Moore |first2=Ronald |date=December 1, 1975 |title=An Analysis of Alpha-Beta Pruning |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0004370275900193 |journal=Artificial Intelligence |publisher=[[Elsevier]] |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=293–326 |doi=10.1016/0004-3702(75)90019-3 |issn=0004-3702 |via=[[ScienceDirect]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Transposition table]]s ([[Mac Hack]] by [[Richard Greenblatt (programmer)|Richard Greenblatt]] in 1966 first used a [[Hash function|hash]]) allowed the program to store the best move for each position and reuse it as the first choice on subsequent visits.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Greenblatt |first=Richard |author-link=Richard Greenblatt (programmer) |title=Computer Chess Compendium |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4757-1968-0_7 |chapter=The Greenblatt Chess Program |date=January 1, 1988 |publisher=[[Springer Nature]] |isbn=978-1-4757-1970-3 |location=New York |pages=56–66 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-1968-0_7}}</ref> In 1968 [[Barbara Liskov]] and others independently suggested storing moves that caused beta cutoffs. This eventually became known as the [[killer heuristic]]. In 1983 [[Jonathan Schaeffer]] proposed the [[history heuristic]]. Schaeffer showed that the history scores outperformed simpler heuristics.

== Theoretical background ==
The efficiency of a [[chess engine]]'s search is almost entirely dependent on its ability to ignore "bad" moves as quickly as possible. Theoretically, if an engine could always examine the best move first, the search space would effectively be reduced to its square root.<ref name=":0" /> This is achieved through a combination of [[game theory]] and heuristic-based pruning.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Campbell |first1=Murray |author-link1=Murray Campbell |last2=Hoane Jr. |first2=A. Joseph |last3=Hsu |first3=Feng-hsiung |author-link3=Feng-hsiung Hsu |date=January 24, 2002 |title=Deep Blue. |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0004370201001291 |journal=Artificial Intelligence |volume=134 |issue=1–2 |pages=57–83 |doi=10.1016/S0004-3702(01)00129-1 |issn=0004-3702 |via=[[ScienceDirect]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

A [[Brute-force search|pure minimax]] game-tree search explores all moves to a fixed depth, which is exponentially expensive.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cormen |first1=Thomas |author-link1=Thomas H. Cormen |title=Introduction to Algorithms |last2=Leiserson |first2=Charles |author-link2=Charles E. Leiserson |last3=Rivest |first3=Ronald |author-link3=Ron Rivest |last4=Stein |first4=Clifford |author-link4=Clifford Stein |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |isbn=978-0-262-04630-5 |edition=4th |publication-date=April 5, 2022 |pages=1020–1032 |lccn=2021037260 |ol=34192801M}}</ref> Alpha–beta pruning improves this by carrying two bounds which are Alpha (α) and Beta (β).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Luger |first=George |title=Artificial Intelligence: Structures and Strategies for Complex Problem Solving |date=February 26, 2008 |publisher=[[Addison-Wesley]] |isbn=978-0321545893 |edition=6th |pages=161–171 |lccn=2007050376 |oclc=439520815 |ol=3946606M}}</ref> Alpha is the minimum score the maximizing player is assured of, and Beta is the maximum score the minimizing player can permit. Whenever a node's value cannot possibly influence the final decision because it is worse than a previously examined move, the branch is cut off. This has a probability to have the same result as full minimax but with fewer nodes.

[[Iterative deepening depth-first search]] is commonly used. The engine repeatedly searches with increasing depth limits, using the best move from depth <math>d</math> as the first move to try at depth <math>d+1</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Russell |first1=Stuart |author-link1=Stuart J. Russell |title=Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach |last2=Norvig |first2=Peter |author-link2=Peter Norvig |date=December 1, 2009 |publisher=[[Prentice Hall]] |isbn=978-0136042594 |edition=3rd |lccn=2011-288031 |oclc=359890490 }}</ref> This almost produces a strong initial bound (alpha or beta) on the first move, which narrows the window for the rest of the search. Iterative deepening converts a depth-first search into something akin to a best-first search by leveraging past results. When a transposition table contains an entry for the current position, its stored best move is tried first.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Silver |first1=David |author-link1=David Silver (computer scientist) |title=Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General Reinforcement Learning Algorithm |date=December 5, 2017 |last2=Hubert |first2=Thomas |last3=Schrittwieser |first3=Julian |last4=Antonoglou |first4=Ioannis |last5=Lai |first5=Matthew |last6=Guez |first6=Arthur |last7=Lanctot |first7=Marc |last8=Sifre |first8=Laurent |last9=Kumaran |first9=Dharshan |author-link9=Dharshan Kumaran |last10=Graepel |first10=Thore |last11=Lillicrap |first11=Timothy |author-link11=Timothy Lillicrap |last12=Simonyan |first12=Karen |last13=Hassabis |first13=Demis |author-link13=Demis Hassabis |eprint=1712.01815v1 |page=10 |class=cs.AI }} ''"A transposition table facilitates the reuse of values and move orders when the same position is reached by multiple paths."''</ref> After a transposition move is considered, typical ordering heuristics prioritize captures and checks, since forcing tactical moves often lead to large advantages or immediate cut offs.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Levy |first1=David |last2=Newborn |first2=Monty |title=How Computers Play Chess |publisher=Computer Science Press |location=New York |year=1991 |edition=1st |pages=144–148 |isbn=0-7167-8239-1 |oclc=826075762 |lccn=90039244 |language=en |url=https://archive.org/details/howcomputersplay0000levy}}</ref>

Engines sort capture moves by the Most Valuable Victim–Least Valuable Aggressor (MVV-LVA) heuristic.<ref name=":2" /> To avoid obviously losing trades, a static exchange evaluation (SEE) is often applied to prune captures that reduce material balance. If the forcing moves do not produce a cutoff, the engine then tries its stored killer moves, which are tried at early depth. If a non-killer move causes a cutoff, it becomes a new killer. Finally, any remaining quiet moves are ordered by their history heuristic scores, which accumulate bonuses when a move causes a cutoff.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schaeffer |first=Jonathan |author-link=Jonathan Schaeffer |date=November 30, 1989 |title=The History Heuristic and the Performance of Alpha-Beta Enhancements |journal=[[IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence]] |volume=11 |issue=11 |pages=1203–1212 |doi=10.1109/34.42858 |issn=0162-8828 |eissn=1939-3539 |oclc=8557794501 }}</ref> Each time a move causes a cutoff anywhere in the search, its history score increases. Thus moves that have historically caused cutoffs rank higher in future ordering.

== Advanced topics ==
Researchers have developed several refinements beyond the basic schemes. Countermove heuristic assumes that many moves have a "natural" response, irrespective of the actual position.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Uiterwijk |first=Jos |date=March 1, 1992 |title=The Countermove Heuristic |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3233/ICG-1992-15103 |journal=[[ICGA Journal]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=8–15 |doi=10.3233/ICG-1992-15103 |issn=1389-6911 |oclc=10597453955 |via=[[Sage Publishing]]|url-access=subscription }} ''"The technique is based on the assumption that many moves have a 'natural' response, irrespective of the actual position in which the moves occur."''</ref> Other miscellaneous techniques such as "Butterfly boards"<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hartmann |first=Dap |date=September 1, 1988 |title=The Butterfly Heuristic |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3233/ICG-1988-112-303 |journal=[[ICGA Journal]] |volume=11 |issue=2–3 |pages=64–71 |doi=10.3233/ICG-1988-112-303 |issn=1389-6911 |via=[[Sage Publishing]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and "last-best-reply" heuristics are related ideas that exploit local search history. Some engines use [[machine learning]], early work by Kocsis et al. and Greer applied [[neural network]]s to predict move values or ordering. Most strong engines still rely on the simple set of PV moves, hash moves, MVV-LVA capture sorting, killer and history tables.
